• 	After a message is polled by a consumer, it becomes invisible to other consumers

Amazon SQS 	- 	Long Polling
• 	When a consumer requests messages from the
queue, it can optionally “wait” for messages to

• 	LongPolling decreases the number of API calls
made to SQS while increasing the efficiency and
reducing latency of your application

content.summary:
## Queues, visibility and idempotency

Standard SQS provides at-least-once delivery. Make business processing idempotent, delete a message only after success, and align or extend the visibility timeout with processing duration.

### Reasoning and trade-offs

The external side effect must be safe to repeat or deduplicated transactionally. A longer timeout reduces premature concurrent retries but does not remove the crash-after-side-effect window. Early deletion can lose work.

### Avoid this trap

Visibility timeout temporarily hides a message; it does not acknowledge successful processing. A dead-letter queue needs monitoring and a redrive process, not just configuration.

### Apply it

A worker charges a customer, crashes before deleting its SQS message, and later receives the message again. What is the best protection against double charging?

**Recommended design:** Use an idempotency key and an atomic business-state check before applying the charge again.

The external side effect must be safe to repeat or deduplicated transactionally. A longer timeout reduces premature concurrent retries but does not remove the crash-after-side-effect window. Early deletion can lose work.

content.supplement: Tutor-authored explanation using architectural knowledge alongside the cited main-source chapter. These are original practice questions, not official AWS exam questions. Supplementary reading is listed separately; vocabulary overlap does not establish factual agreement.

cards.question: What delivery model does standard SQS use?
Does a visibility timeout acknowledge processing success?
cards.answer: No. Delete the message after successful processing.

quiz.question: A worker charges a customer, crashes before deleting its SQS message, and later receives the message again. What is the best protection against double charging?
options: Set a longer visibility timeout and assume duplicates become impossible.
Delete every message before starting the charge operation.
Use an idempotency key and an atomic business-state check before applying the charge again.
Use a dead-letter queue as the only record of completed charges.
quiz.explanation: The external side effect must be safe to repeat or deduplicated transactionally. A longer timeout reduces premature concurrent retries but does not remove the crash-after-side-effect window. Early deletion can lose work.

content.summary:
## Fan-out versus replayable streams

SNS with separate SQS queues supports independent durable subscriber backlogs. Kinesis Data Streams supports ordered records within a shard and replay by consumers within configured retention.

### Reasoning and trade-offs

Separate queues give each subscriber its own delivery and retry lifecycle. One shared queue load-balances messages instead of ensuring all services see all events. If retained ordered replay were central, a stream might be the better abstraction.

### Avoid this trap

A single shared queue distributes work among consumers rather than broadcasting every event to every service. Stream ordering is scoped, and capacity/partition-key choices affect throughput.

### Apply it

Billing, fraud and analytics services must each receive every order event and handle backlogs independently. They do not require ordered replay from one shared log. Which design is suitable?

**Recommended design:** Publish to SNS and subscribe a separate SQS queue for each service.

Separate queues give each subscriber its own delivery and retry lifecycle. One shared queue load-balances messages instead of ensuring all services see all events. If retained ordered replay were central, a stream might be the better abstraction.

cards.question: How can every subscriber get an independent durable backlog?
cards.answer: SNS fan-out to a separate SQS queue per subscriber.

cards.question: What does one queue shared by competing consumers do?
cards.answer: Distributes work; it does not broadcast every event to each consumer.

options: Have all three services compete for messages in one standard SQS queue.
Use an ALB target group as the durable event backlog.
Write events only to the memory of the order-service instance.
Publish to SNS and subscribe a separate SQS queue for each service.
